1.title: Know the words and the kinds of writing work
1.intro: Freelance writing means writing for pay for different clients. Start with the basic words and the work.
pts: Learn the terms: pitch, brief, draft, edit, byline, deadline, rate, kill fee, invoice.
Kinds of work: articles, web pages, newsletters, reports, product text.
Name one kind of client and one topic you know well.
Read five paid pieces and note the reader, length and style.
1.ex: Topic: home energy savings. Clients: a local energy firm's blog, a community newsletter, a magazine.
1.act: Read five paid pieces and fill a table of reader, length and style. Write your niche in one line.
1.std: Task: study five pieces. Condition: public pages. Standard: table complete and niche fits one line.

2.title: Explain how a writing job runs
2.intro: A job has steps. If you can name them, you can plan your time and avoid surprises.
pts: The steps: pitch, brief, research, outline, draft, edit, submit, revise, invoice.
A brief says reader, goal, length, tone, deadline and sources.
Ask questions before you write.
Agree how many rounds of changes are included.
2.ex: An editor asks for 800 words on heat pumps for homeowners. You ask: reader, tone, sources, deadline, pay.
2.act: Write a one-page brief form with ten questions.
2.std: Task: complete a brief for a pretend client. Condition: in one 30-minute conversation. Standard: brief states reader, goal, length, tone, deadline and rounds.

3.title: Write a clear piece to a standard
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Write a piece that is clear, true and easy to read.
pts: Put the main point first and use short words.
Write three title options and pick the clearest.
Use facts you can check and name your sources.
Read aloud and cut every useless word.
3.ex: Before: 'Heat pumps are a very interesting option.' After: 'A heat pump can cut your heating bill. Here is how it works.'
3.act: Write a 600-word article and edit it twice.
3.std: Task: write one article. Condition: from a brief, in two hours. Standard: one point, checkable facts, no spelling errors; second draft shorter and clearer.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for writers
4.intro: Copyright, honest claims and privacy rules apply. Learn which ones touch your work.
pts: You own what you write unless a contract says otherwise; do not copy others' text.
Quote briefly and name the source; do not present others' ideas as yours.
Advertising and sponsored posts must be truthful and clearly marked.
Personal information in your story falls under privacy law; ask consent. Check the current rules.
4.ex: A client asks you to write 'Best in Canada'. You ask for proof; there is none, so you write a claim you can verify.
4.act: Make a table of rule, what you must do and where you checked, for ten situations.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unclear cases say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price your work and check it pays
5.intro: You are paid for results and time. Work out your cost per hour and what a project must earn.
pts: Time includes research, calls, drafting, edits and admin.
Hourly cost = yearly costs and needed pay, divided by hours you can really bill.
Compare per-word, per-hour and per-project pricing.
Collect sales tax once registered; check the small-supplier limit with the tax agency.
5.ex: An article takes 5 hours at 45 USD an hour: 225 USD. That is 0.28 per word at 800 words. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Time three pieces from start to finish and set a price for each.
5.std: Task: price three projects. Condition: from your time log. Standard: hours, rate and total shown; a mentor can follow.

6.title: Find clients and show proof
6.intro: Clients hire writers they trust. Build a small portfolio and a steady way to be found.
pts: Make three samples that match the clients you want.
Get written permission before showing client work.
Send ten specific pitches, each with one idea for that client.
Keep a list of contact, date, reply and next step.
6.ex: You pitch a local newsletter: 'Three ways renters can cut winter bills. 500 words.' You attach a short outline.
6.act: Send ten pitches in two weeks and log replies.
6.std: Task: run a two-week outreach. Condition: with consent rules met. Standard: ten pitches sent, replies logged, one lesson written.

7.title: Protect ownership, privacy and quality
7.intro: A professional writer is careful with rights, secrets and facts.
pts: Write down who owns the text and what the client may do with it. Ask a legal adviser for large deals.
Do not copy; use your own words or licensed text.
Keep client files safe with strong passwords and backups.
Fact-check names, prices, dates and quotes.
7.ex: Your contract says: 'The client owns the final text once paid in full. The writer may show it in a portfolio.'
7.act: Write a one-page agreement and a delivery checklist.
7.std: Task: produce both. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: scope, fees, rounds, rights and payment date are clear.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Take jobs, measure and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day goal, such as three paid pieces and one repeat client.
Every week record hours, income, late payments and feedback.
Ask each client for a short review.
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After 60 days: 4 pieces, 24 hours, 900 USD billed, one repeat client. You raise your rate.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real clients, paid or agreed work. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is a pitch?
A short offer of an idea to a client.
What does a brief state?
Reader, goal, length, tone, deadline and sources.
Why write three titles?
To pick the clearest.
Who owns your text?
You, unless a contract says otherwise.
What must sponsored posts do?
Be truthful and clearly marked.
How do you find your hourly cost?
Yearly costs plus needed pay, divided by billable hours.
Why get permission before showing client work?
It belongs to the client unless the agreement says otherwise.
What should an agreement list?
Scope, fees, rounds, rights, payment date and privacy.
What do you check before delivering?
Facts, names, prices, spelling and links.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
